findings.owner: A database change could break the live app while it updates.
findings.title: Migration drops a column
findings.why: It drops a column. A version of the app that still reads that column, including tabs your users already have open, starts failing the moment it runs, and the data in the column is gone. The safe order is to ship a release that stops using the column, then drop it in a later migration. A migration that has been applied cannot be undone, so this is reported to catch the next one before it ships.

fix.text: Add a step to CI that fails a pull request whose new migrations are not backward-compatible. This one checks the migrations a pull request adds for the same patterns this check looks for, and fails too when it cannot check one.

snippet.code:
# .github/workflows/migration-check.yml
name: migration-check
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ['supabase/migrations/**']
jobs:
  migrations:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: New migrations are backward-compatible
        shell: bash
        run: |
          list=$(mktemp)
          if ! git diff -z --name-only --diff-filter=A "origin/${{ github.base_ref }}...HEAD" -- 'supabase/migrations/*.sql' > "$list"; then
            echo "::error::Could not list the migrations this pull request adds."
            exit 1
          fi
          status=0
          while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
            rc=0
            perl -e '
              my $file = shift;
              open(my $fh, "<", $file) or exit 2;
              my $hit = 0;
              while (my $line = <$fh>) {
                chomp $line;
                if ($line =~ /\bdrop\s+(column|table)\b|\brename\s+(column|to)\b|\bset\s+not\s+null\b|\balter\s+column\s+\S+\s+(set\s+data\s+)?type\b|\badd\s+column\b(?![^;,]*\b(default|generated\s+always)\b)[^;,]*\bnot\s+null\b|\btruncate\b/i) { print "$file:$.:$line\n"; $hit = 1; }
              }
              close($fh) or exit 2;
              exit $hit;
            ' -- "$file" || rc=$?
            if [ "$rc" -eq 1 ]; then
              echo "::error file=$file::$file is not backward-compatible: it drops, renames, retypes or truncates, or adds a required column without a default. Split it into backward-compatible steps."
              status=1
            elif [ "$rc" -ne 0 ]; then
              echo "::error file=$file::Could not check $file: perl exited $rc."
              status=1
            fi
          done < "$list"
          exit "$status"

findings.checkBefore: Whether this migration has already been applied to production. If it has, confirm the live app no longer depends on what it changed. If it has not, split it into backward-compatible steps before applying it.

findings.title: Rotate the Supabase service-role key eyJhbG…81IU found in the git history
findings.why: Rotate this key: it is in the git history at 040f259 src/integrations/supabase/admin.ts, and the history keeps it after any fix; the tool cannot see whether you rotated it.

fix.text: In the Supabase dashboard, Project Settings, API Keys: move everything that uses the legacy anon and service_role keys to the new publishable and secret keys, then disable the legacy keys. Disabling them does not stop this key: it still works when sent as an Authorization: Bearer token. To stop it, in Project Settings, JWT Keys, move to the new JWT signing keys, then revoke the legacy JWT secret. If you keep the legacy keys instead, roll the legacy JWT secret, which replaces the anon key too. Rewriting the history does not help: every clone and fork already has the key.

findings.checkBefore: Every place that uses this key (servers, edge functions, CI, local env files), so you can give them the new one before the old one stops working.

findings.title: Leaked password protection is on
findings.why: It refuses passwords known from public data breaches, which are the first ones attackers try. The tool cannot read the live project's auth settings without the Management API, which it never uses.

fix.text: In the Supabase dashboard, Authentication, Attack Protection: turn on leaked password protection.

findings.checkBefore: That your sign-up and password-reset forms show the error the API returns when a password is refused.

findings.title: Minimum password length is at least 8
findings.why: Short passwords fall to guessing quickly. The tool cannot read the live project's auth settings without the Management API, which it never uses.

fix.text: In the Supabase dashboard, Authentication, Attack Protection: set the minimum password length to 8 or more.

findings.checkBefore: That your sign-up form's own validation and message match the new minimum. Existing passwords keep working.

findings.title: Confirm email is on

location.object: Supabase dashboard: Authentication > Sign In / Providers > Email

findings.why: Without email confirmation, anyone can sign up with an address they do not own, and the account works at once. The tool cannot read the live project's auth settings without the Management API, which it never uses.

fix.text: In the Supabase dashboard, Authentication, Sign In / Providers, Email: turn on Confirm email.

findings.checkBefore: That your sign-up flow tells users to check their inbox, and that the link in the email goes to an allowed redirect URL.

findings.title: Secure email change is on

location.object: Supabase dashboard: Authentication > Sign In / Providers > Email

findings.why: Without it, a new email address needs confirming only from the new address, so someone with brief access to a signed-in session can move the account to an inbox they control. The tool cannot read the live project's auth settings without the Management API, which it never uses.

fix.text: In the Supabase dashboard, Authentication, Sign In / Providers, Email: turn on Secure email change.

findings.checkBefore: How users who can no longer reach their old inbox will change their address: they will need your support.

findings.title: Site URL and redirect URLs list only the app's own domains
findings.why: Sign-in links, password resets and OAuth sign-ins send users, with their session, to these URLs. A broad wildcard or a domain you do not control lets someone else receive a session. The tool cannot read the live project's auth settings without the Management API, which it never uses.

fix.text: In the Supabase dashboard, Authentication, URL Configuration: set Site URL to the app's production address, and list in Redirect URLs only the app's own domains (and localhost while developing), without broad wildcards.

findings.checkBefore: Every redirectTo and emailRedirectTo your app passes, so each one is still on the list.

findings.title: Auth emails go through your own SMTP server

location.object: Supabase dashboard: Authentication > Emails > SMTP Settings

findings.why: Supabase's built-in email service is for testing only: it sends about 2 emails an hour, and only to your project's team members, so real users get no sign-up, password reset or sign-in emails. The tool cannot read the live project's auth settings without the Management API, which it never uses.

fix.text: In the Supabase dashboard, Authentication, Emails, SMTP Settings: turn on custom SMTP and enter your email provider's details. With Resend, for example: host smtp.resend.com, port 465, user resend, a Resend API key as the password, and a sender address on a domain you have verified in Resend. Any SMTP provider works.

findings.checkBefore: That the sender address is on a domain verified with the provider (see the manual check on SPF, DKIM and DMARC), then send yourself a password reset to test it. Supabase starts custom SMTP with a low hourly email limit, which you can raise under Authentication, Rate Limits.

findings.title: The sending domain has SPF, DKIM and DMARC records
findings.why: Without them, inbox providers such as Gmail and Outlook treat your auth emails as possibly forged and send them to spam or refuse them, so users never see their confirmation or reset link. The tool reads only the repo and the database, and a domain's DNS records are in neither.

fix.text: At your domain's DNS host, add the records your email provider lists. With Resend, for example: add the domain under Domains, add the SPF and DKIM records it shows, and wait until it shows as verified. Then add a DMARC record: a TXT record named _dmarc with the value v=DMARC1; p=none; and change p=none to p=quarantine once your emails are arriving.

findings.checkBefore: Any SPF record the domain already has, for example for its own mailboxes: a domain may have only one, so add the provider to it rather than adding a second.

findings.title: The project is on a paid plan, with daily backups
findings.why: The free plan keeps no backups and pauses a project after a week without activity. A paused app is offline until someone restores it, and data lost to a bad change cannot be brought back. The tool cannot see which plan the project is on.

fix.text: Move the organization to the Pro plan or above before launch. Paid projects are backed up daily and are not paused for inactivity.

findings.checkBefore: If the project is already on a paid plan, open Database > Backups in the dashboard and check that it lists a backup from the last day.
